summary: Specifies IANA registration procedures for MIME external body access types and content transfer encodings. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: MIME lets different kinds of content travel in one email message, and it is built so that new kinds can be added without changing the protocol itself. This document explains how a new kind is proposed, what it has to describe for anyone to be able to implement it, and how it ends up in the public list of registered names.

questions: how to register a mime transfer encoding
what is a mime external body access type
subtitle: How new MIME access types and transfer encodings get registered, and what a proposal must satisfy.

tldr.problem: MIME is an open-ended framework, so anyone can add a new object type, charset or access method to it, and the protocol itself needs no change. Without a process, the set of such values would grow in an ad hoc way.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets out the requirements a new access type or transfer encoding must meet, and the procedure that takes a proposal from an Internet-Draft through public review to registration by IANA.
tldr.outcome: It defines two IANA registries, one for external body access types and one for transfer encodings, and it obsoletes RFC 2048. Media type registration moved to RFC 4288 and charset registration to RFC 2978.

sections.title: Why MIME Needs a Registration Process
sections.content:
Recent Internet protocols have been carefully designed to be easily extensible in certain areas. MIME in particular is an open-ended framework and can accommodate additional object types, charsets and access methods without any changes to the basic protocol. A registration process is needed, however, to ensure that the set of such values is developed in an orderly, well-specified and public manner.

This document defines registration procedures that use the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) as a central registry for these values. The registration of media types and charsets for use in MIME is specified in separate documents and is not addressed here.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME was designed to grow. Something has to keep the list of registered names in order and public, and that is what this document sets up, using IANA as the registry.

sections.title: External Body Access Types
sections.content:
RFC 2046 defines the message/external-body media type, whereby a MIME entity can act as a pointer to the actual body data instead of including the data directly in the entity body. Each message/external-body reference specifies an access type, which determines the mechanism used to retrieve the actual body data.

RFC 2046 defines an initial set of access types, but allows for the registration of additional access types to accommodate new retrieval mechanisms. A registered access type is therefore the name of a way to fetch the body of a message: the name appears in the access-type parameter of the message/external-body content-type header field.
sections.plainLanguage: A message can point at its real content instead of carrying it. The pointer names an access type, and the access type says how to fetch the content, for example from a file or a web server.

sections.title: What a New Access Type Must Satisfy
sections.content:
New access type specifications MUST conform to four sets of requirements.

  • Naming. Each access type MUST have a unique name. This name appears in the access-type parameter in the message/external-body content-type header field and MUST conform to MIME content type parameter syntax.
  • Mechanism specification. All of the protocols, transports and procedures used by a given access type MUST be described, either in the specification of the access type itself or in some other publicly available specification, in sufficient detail for the access type to be implemented by any competent implementor. The use of secret and proprietary methods in access types is expressly prohibited. The restrictions imposed by RFC 2026 on the standardization of patented algorithms must be respected as well.
  • Publication. All access types MUST be described by an RFC. The RFC may be informational rather than standards-track, although standards-track review and approval are encouraged for all access types.
  • Security. Any known security issues that arise from the use of the access type MUST be completely and fully described. It is not required that the access type be secure or that it be free from risks, but it is required that the known risks be identified. Publication of a new access type does not require an exhaustive security review, and the security considerations section is subject to continuing evaluation. Additional security considerations SHOULD be addressed by publishing revised versions of the access type specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A proposal has to have a unique name, has to describe its mechanism in enough detail that someone else could build it without asking the author anything, has to be published as an RFC, and has to say what its known risks are. It does not have to be risk-free, but the risks have to be written down.

sections.title: Registering an Access Type
sections.content:
Registration of a new access type starts with the publication of the specification as an Internet Draft. A proposed access type specification is then sent to the ietf-types@iana.org mailing list for a two-week review period. This mailing list has been established for the purpose of reviewing proposed access and media types. Proposed access types are not formally registered and must not be used. The intent of the public posting is to solicit comments and feedback on the access type specification and a review of any security considerations.

When the two-week period has passed, the access type reviewer, who is appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director, either forwards the request to IANA or rejects it because of significant objections raised on the list. Decisions made by the reviewer must be posted to the mailing list within 14 days, and may be appealed to the IESG as specified in RFC 2026.

Provided that the access type either has passed review or has been successfully appealed to the IESG, IANA will register the access type and make the registration available to the community. The specification of the access type must also be published as an RFC.

The identity of the access type reviewer is communicated to IANA by the IESG. IANA then acts only in response to access type definitions that are approved by the reviewer and forwarded to it, or in response to a communication from the IESG that an appeal has overturned the reviewer's ruling. The list of registered access types is published by IANA in the access types registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The route is: write the draft, post it to a mailing list for two weeks of public review, then a named reviewer either forwards it to IANA or rejects it. Either way the decision is posted to the list within a fortnight, and a rejected proposal can be appealed to the IESG.

sections.title: What Transfer Encodings Are For
sections.content:
Transfer encodings are transformations applied to MIME media types after conversion to the media type's canonical form. They are used for several purposes.

  • Many transports, especially message transports, can only handle data consisting of relatively short lines of text, and there can be severe restrictions on what characters can be used in those lines. Some transports are restricted to a small subset of US-ASCII, and others cannot handle certain character sequences. Transfer encodings are used to transform binary data into a textual form that can survive such transports. The base64 and quoted-printable transfer encodings are examples of this.
  • Image, audio, video and even application entities are sometimes quite large. Compression algorithms are often effective in reducing the size of large entities, and transfer encodings can be used to apply general-purpose non-lossy compression algorithms to MIME entities.
  • Transfer encodings can be defined as a means of representing existing encoding formats in a MIME context.

The document states that the standardization of a large number of different transfer encodings is seen as a significant barrier to widespread interoperability and is expressly discouraged. Nevertheless, the procedure has been defined in order to provide a means of defining additional transfer encodings, should standardization actually be justified.
sections.plainLanguage: A transfer encoding is a transformation applied to the content of a MIME part, usually to make it survive a transport that only handles simple text, and sometimes to shrink it. The document warns that adding many such encodings is a barrier to interoperability, so the bar for adding one is deliberately high.

sections.title: What a New Transfer Encoding Must Satisfy
sections.content:
Transfer encoding specifications MUST conform to seven sets of requirements.

  • Naming. Each transfer encoding MUST have a unique name. This name appears in the Content-Transfer-Encoding header field and MUST conform to the syntax of that field.
  • Algorithm specification. All of the algorithms used in a transfer encoding, for example conversion to printable form or compression, MUST be described in their entirety in the transfer encoding specification. The use of secret and proprietary algorithms in standardized transfer encodings is expressly prohibited, and the restrictions imposed by RFC 2026 on the standardization of patented algorithms MUST be respected.
  • Input domain. All transfer encodings MUST be applicable to an arbitrary sequence of octets of any length, and dependence on particular input forms is not allowed. The document notes that the 7bit and 8bit encodings do not conform to this requirement, and that the intent is to forbid the addition of further encodings similar to or redundant with them.
  • Output range. There is no requirement that a particular transfer encoding produce a particular form of encoded output, but the output format MUST be fully and completely documented. Each specification MUST clearly state whether the output format always lies within the confines of 7bit or 8bit, or is simply pure binary data.
  • Data integrity and generality. All transfer encodings MUST be fully invertible on any platform; it MUST be possible for anyone to recover the original data by performing the corresponding decoding operation. This requirement effectively excludes all forms of lossy compression as well as all forms of encryption from use as a transfer encoding.
  • New functionality. All transfer encodings MUST provide some sort of new functionality. Some degree of functionality overlap with previously defined transfer encodings is acceptable, but any new transfer encoding MUST also offer something no other transfer encoding provides.
  • Security. To the greatest extent possible, transfer encodings SHOULD NOT contain known security issues. Regardless, any known security issues that arise from the use of the transfer encoding MUST be completely and fully described, and issues that come to light after publication SHOULD be addressed by publishing revised versions of the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for a transfer encoding are strict on purpose. It must work on any bytes at all, it must be exactly reversible so that nothing is lost or hidden, and it must do something no existing encoding already does.

sections.title: Defining a Transfer Encoding
sections.content:
Definition of a new transfer encoding starts with the publication of the specification as an Internet Draft. The draft MUST define the transfer encoding precisely and completely, and it MUST also provide substantial justification for defining and standardizing a new transfer encoding. The specification MUST then be presented to the IESG for consideration. The IESG can reject the specification outright as being inappropriate for standardization, assign the specification to an existing IETF working group for further work, approve the formation of an IETF working group to work on the specification in accordance with IETF procedures, or accept the specification as-is for processing as an individual standards-track submission.

Transfer encoding specifications on the standards track follow the normal IETF rules for standards-track documents, and a transfer encoding is considered to be defined and available for use once it is on the standards track.

There is no need for a special procedure for registering transfer encodings with IANA. All legitimate transfer encoding registrations MUST appear as a standards-track RFC, so it is the IESG's responsibility to notify IANA when a new transfer encoding has been approved. The list of transfer encoding registrations is published by IANA in the transfer encodings registry.
sections.plainLanguage: A new transfer encoding has to go through the full IETF process, because it has to end up on the standards track before anyone may use it. The IESG decides whether to reject it, hand it to a working group, or take it forward as a submission.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security requirements for access types are set out in the access type requirements section, and the security requirements for transfer encodings in the transfer encoding requirements section. Both require that the known security issues of the new name be described completely and fully, and both allow a specification to be revised later if new issues appear.

The IANA considerations section states that the sole purpose of the document is to define IANA registries for access types and transfer encodings, with the IANA procedures for these registries specified in Sections 2.4 and 3.3 respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: Both kinds of registry entry carry the same rule about security: write down the known risks. The registries themselves are the IANA access types list and the IANA transfer encodings list.

viz.caption: THE FOUR REQUIREMENTS FOR A NEW ACCESS TYPE

items.title: Naming
items.text: A unique name that fits the syntax of the access-type parameter.

items.title: Mechanism specification
items.text: Every protocol, transport and procedure described in enough detail to implement; no secret or proprietary methods.

items.title: Publication
items.text: Described by an RFC, which may be informational rather than standards-track.

items.title: Security
items.text: Known security issues fully described; the entry need not be risk-free, but its risks must be identified.

viz.caption: THE STEPS OF AN ACCESS TYPE REGISTRATION

items.title: Publish an Internet-Draft
items.text: The registration process starts with the specification as a draft.

items.title: Two-week public review
items.text: The draft is posted to the ietf-types mailing list for comments.

items.title: The reviewer decides
items.text: The access type reviewer forwards it to IANA or rejects it, and posts that decision within 14 days.

items.title: Appeal is possible
items.text: A decision may be appealed to the IESG.

items.title: IANA registers
items.text: Registration happens once review has passed or an appeal has succeeded, and the specification is published as an RFC.

viz.caption: THE THREE USES OF A TRANSFER ENCODING

cells: Turns binary data into a textual form that a message transport can carry
Applies a general-purpose non-lossy compression algorithm to a MIME entity
Expresses an encoding format that already exists in a MIME context

viz.caption: THE SEVEN REQUIREMENTS FOR A NEW TRANSFER ENCODING

items.title: Naming
items.text: A unique name that fits the syntax of the Content-Transfer-Encoding field.

items.title: Algorithm specification
items.text: Every algorithm described in full; no secret or proprietary algorithms.

items.title: Input domain
items.text: Must apply to any sequence of octets of any length.

items.title: Output range
items.text: The output format must be documented, and must say whether it is 7bit, 8bit or binary.

items.title: Data integrity
items.text: Must be exactly reversible on any platform, which rules out lossy compression and encryption.

items.title: New functionality
items.text: Must offer something no existing transfer encoding offers.

items.title: Security
items.text: Known issues fully described, and revised versions published when new ones appear.
